structure.name: Skull Structure
structure.desc: Baby's skull consists of multiple bone plates connected by "cranial sutures", allowing the head to grow with brain development.

fontanelles.name: Fontanelle Closure
fontanelles.desc: The posterior fontanelle (small soft spot at the back) usually closes around 2 months, while the anterior fontanelle (soft spot at the top) typically closes at 12-18 months.

plasticity.desc: Since the skull hasn't closed yet, posture greatly affects head shape.

classification.title: Common Head Shape Variations
classification.subtitle: Most head shape variations are normal developmental changes. Understanding their characteristics helps with proper care
classification.reminder_title: Positional Head Shape Changes Are Normal
classification.reminder_content: Most head shape changes are positional and improve naturally by adjusting sleep positions, increasing tummy time, and other simple methods - no need to worry excessively
classification.reminder_note: 💡 Tip: Regularly vary baby's sleeping and play positions to encourage natural head shape development
classification.medical_warning_title: Pathological Head Shapes Require Medical Attention
classification.medical_warning_content: Pathological head shapes (such as scaphocephaly) cannot be treated through sleep position adjustments or corrective helmets. These conditions require professional medical diagnosis and surgical treatment. If severe head shape abnormalities, abnormal head circumference growth, or other symptoms are observed, immediate consultation with a pediatrician or cranial specialist for professional evaluation is essential.

normal.name: Normal Head Shape
normal.description: Head shows natural rounded shape with basic symmetry front-to-back and left-to-right, meeting normal developmental standards.
normal.causes: Normal fetal development and appropriate position changes after birth, with skull forming ideal shape during natural growth process.
normal.correction: No special intervention needed, continue good care habits, regular position changes, ensure healthy development.

brachycephaly.name: Brachycephaly
brachycephaly.image_alt: Brachycephaly example image showing flattened back of head characteristics
brachycephaly.description: Flattening of the back of the head, the most common head shape variation in infancy, typically peaking at 7-12 weeks of age.
brachycephaly.causes: Primarily caused by supine sleeping position. The AAP recommends back sleeping to reduce SIDS risk, but it may affect head shape.
brachycephaly.correction: Over 80% of babies naturally improve by age 2. Recommendations: more tummy time when awake, alternate sleep positions, reduce lying flat time.

plagiocephaly.name: Plagiocephaly
plagiocephaly.image_alt: Plagiocephaly example image showing asymmetrical head shape with one side flattened
plagiocephaly.description: One side of the head is relatively flat, showing asymmetrical appearance. This condition typically peaks at 4 months and then begins to improve.
plagiocephaly.causes: Common with preferential side sleeping and intrauterine position restrictions. 70%-95% of babies with asymmetrical heads have mild torticollis, which is normal.
plagiocephaly.correction: Most cases improve naturally. Recommendations: encourage turning to the other side, increase tummy time, gentle neck exercises.

dolichocephaly.name: Dolichocephaly
dolichocephaly.image_alt: Dolichocephaly example image showing elongated head shape that is longer front-to-back and narrower on sides
dolichocephaly.description: Head is longer front-to-back and relatively narrower on the sides, but with normal open sutures. Common in premature infants or babies who lie on their sides for extended periods.
dolichocephaly.causes: Primarily caused by prolonged side-lying position, common in NICU premature infants. Unlike pathological scaphocephaly, suture development is normal.
dolichocephaly.correction: Most cases can improve naturally with position adjustments. Recommendations: reduce side-lying time, increase supine and prone time, head massage.

scaphocephaly.name: Scaphocephaly
scaphocephaly.image_alt: Pathological scaphocephaly example image showing boat-shaped skull caused by premature sagittal suture closure
scaphocephaly.description: Caused by premature sagittal suture closure, characterized by a prominent bony ridge running from front to back on top of the head, with pointed front and back, resembling a boat shape, the most common type of craniosynostosis.
scaphocephaly.causes: Premature fusion of sagittal suture prevents lateral skull growth while anteroposterior growth continues, forming an elongated narrow head. Male incidence is 3 times higher than female.
scaphocephaly.correction: Pathological scaphocephaly is a form of craniosynostosis that must be treated through neurosurgical intervention and cannot be improved through conservative methods such as sleep position adjustments, physical therapy, or corrective helmets. Surgery typically involves removal of the fused sagittal suture and skull reshaping, with better outcomes from early diagnosis and surgical treatment, requiring evaluation and treatment by specialized neurosurgeons

sleep.title: Sleep & Tummy Time Guide
sleep.subtitle: Scientifically guiding baby's posture to prevent and improve positional head shape issues

principle1.name: Safety First, Scientific Care
principle1.desc: Always follow safe sleep guidelines. Back sleeping significantly reduces SIDS risk. Never place babies on their stomach to sleep - safety must always come first.

principle2.name: Frequent Position Changes, Even Pressure Distribution
principle2.desc: Newborn skulls are soft and moldable, making them susceptible to flattening from prolonged fixed positions. Rotate between left side, right side, and back sleeping to distribute pressure evenly and encourage natural head rounding.

principle3.name: Appropriate Mattress, Stable Support
principle3.desc: Select a firm mattress that provides proper support without excessive sinking. Soft mattresses can create uneven pressure on your baby's head, causing one side to sink in and potentially leading to flat spots or asymmetry, while also hindering healthy spinal development.

principle4.name: Careful Observation, Timely Adjustment
principle4.desc: The first 6 months are crucial for head shape development. Monitor your baby's head shape closely and adjust care practices immediately if you notice flattening or asymmetry. After 6 months, increased mobility naturally helps round out the head shape.

sleep.newborn_desc: Focus on sleep position changes, avoid prolonged supine position, adjust head position every 2 hours
sleep.infant_desc: Increase tummy time, start neck exercises, pay attention to head shape symmetry
sleep.toddler_desc: Encourage various sleep positions, reduce prolonged fixed postures, focus on final head shape formation
sleep.mobile_desc: Babies begin to roll over and sit up, head shape is basically set, focus shifts to maintenance and prevention of bad habits

technique1.name: Tummy Time Practice
technique1.desc: Start from the newborn period with 3-5 supervised tummy time sessions daily, 2-5 minutes each. This relieves pressure on the back of the head, strengthens neck muscles, and prevents flat head syndrome. Always use a firm, flat surface and ensure clear breathing

technique2.name: Varied Feeding Positions
technique2.desc: Alternate between cradle hold, football hold, and side-lying positions. Switch arms with each feeding to prevent prolonged pressure on one side of the head while promoting visual and spatial development

technique3.name: Environmental Encouragement
technique3.desc: Strategically arrange your baby's environment by regularly moving toys, music boxes, or colorful patterns around the crib to encourage natural head turning. Every few days, alternate which end of the crib your baby's head faces, so light and visual stimuli naturally draw their attention in different directions.

technique4.name: Side Sleeping Tips
technique4.desc: When positioning your baby on their side, ensure both head and body face the same direction—never just turn the head while keeping the body straight. This misalignment strains the neck and can worsen head asymmetry. Use a rolled towel or small pillow behind your baby's back for support, and remember to alternate between left and right sides.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.subtitle: Common questions about using LunaSphere

about.question: What is LunaSphere?
about.answer:
LunaSphere is a free tool for checking your baby's head shape at home.

The Cephalic Index (CI) and Cranial Vault Asymmetry Index (CVAI) are standard clinical measurements used worldwide to assess infant head shape—CI for flatness/elongation, CVAI for left-right symmetry. We want to bring this expertise to every family—just snap a photo at home, and feel confident knowing how your little one is developing.

notMedical.question: Is this a medical diagnosis?
notMedical.answer:
LunaSphere is a home screening tool that helps you understand your baby's head shape—but it's not a substitute for a doctor's diagnosis.

• Hospital assessment: Professional equipment, doctor diagnosis, official reports
• LunaSphere: Free, convenient, great for tracking changes over time

We're here to help ease unnecessary worry, and give you confidence when it's time to seek professional advice.

privacy.question: Are my photos uploaded?
privacy.answer:
No. All photo analysis happens locally on your device—nothing is uploaded to any server.

Photos are cleared from memory immediately after analysis. We take your baby's privacy seriously.

photoTips.question: How do I take a good photo?
photoTips.answer:
Good photos lead to accurate results:

• Angle: Shoot straight down from above, camera parallel to baby's head
• Lighting: Soft and even, avoid harsh shadows
• Hair: Best results right after bath when hair is wet and flat
• Background: Simple and clean
• Position: Baby lying relaxed, head natural

detectionFailed.question: What if detection fails?
detectionFailed.answer:
No worries—it's usually just a photo issue. A quick adjustment should help:

• Make sure the full head outline is visible
• Check that lighting is bright and even
• Shoot straight down, not from the side
• Use a plain background

If it still doesn't work after a few tries, the "Profile Match" feature is a great visual alternative.

whatIsCICVAI.question: What are CI and CVAI?
whatIsCICVAI.answer:
Two head shape measurements:

**CI (Cephalic Index)**
Head width ÷ length—shows if the head is flat or long. Normal range: 76-90%. Below 76% is elongated, above 90% is flat.

**CVAI (Cranial Vault Asymmetry Index)**
Difference between diagonal measurements—shows symmetry. < 3.5% normal, 3.5-7% mild, 7-12% moderate, > 12% severe asymmetry.

abnormalResult.question: What if results seem abnormal?
abnormalResult.answer:
Don't panic—most head shape issues can improve with proper care.

Mild cases usually just need consistent daily care; moderate cases need closer attention and a doctor visit if no improvement; severe cases should see a pediatrician soon.

The first 6 months are the best window for improvement. Visit [Parent Academy](/learn) for detailed guidance and care tips—we're here to help you through this journey.

howOften.question: How often should I measure?
howOften.answer:
Every 2-4 weeks to track trends.

• 0-6 months: Changes fast—every 2 weeks
• 6-12 months: Slowing down—monthly
• After 12 months: Mostly stable—as needed

We know you want to keep a close eye on your little one, but head shape changes gradually. Measuring too often can add stress over tiny variations. Take it easy—focus on the trend.

We recommend using your phone for the easiest photo-taking experience. No download needed.

references.aapTummyTime: The AAP recommends starting tummy time right after coming home, working up to 15-30 minutes daily by 7 weeks.
references.aapSafeSleep: Back sleeping is the safest way to prevent SIDS. Keep the sleep area free of pillows and soft items.
references.aapNoPillow: Soft items like pillows can block a baby's airway—they're the leading cause of accidental suffocation in infants.
references.fontanelleClosure: The back soft spot typically closes by 6-8 weeks; the top one closes between 12-18 months.
references.plagiocephalyTiming: Flat spots usually look worst around 4-5 months. If there's no improvement by 4 months, it's time to see a specialist.
references.helmetTherapy: Helmet therapy works best when started at 5-6 months. It's effective up to 12 months, but results drop off significantly after that.
references.cranialGrowth: 85% of skull growth happens in the first year—that's why early intervention matters.
references.feedingPositions: Switching up feeding positions and arms helps even out pressure on baby's head and builds balanced neck muscles.
references.repositioning: Use your baby's natural curiosity: place toys on the rounder side and position the crib so they turn toward interesting things.
references.deviceTime: Limit time in car seats, bouncers, and carriers. Holding baby upright or tummy-down on your arm gives their head a break.

timeline.title: Your Baby's Head Shape Journey
timeline.subtitle: What to expect at each stage and how you can help

stage1.title: Newborn
stage1.highlights: Baby's skull is very soft with flexible joints between the bones. Any odd shape from birth usually rounds out within days. The back soft spot starts closing.
stage1.tips: Now's the time to build good habits. Start tummy time within days of birth—even 5-10 minutes a day helps. Switch which way baby's head faces during sleep.

stage2.title: Prime Window
stage2.highlights: The back soft spot closes. Baby starts holding their head up as neck muscles get stronger. This is your best chance to improve head shape—most flat spots can get much better now.
stage2.tips: Aim for 30-40 minutes of tummy time daily. Encourage baby to look toward their less-favorite side. Flat spots often look worst around 4 months—if you're not seeing improvement, talk to your doctor. Helmet therapy works best when started at 5-6 months.

stage3.title: Active Phase
stage3.highlights: The skull is firming up but still has some flexibility. As baby sits and crawls, they spend less time on their back, and head shape often improves on its own. Most skull growth (85%) is done by 12 months.
stage3.tips: Keep baby active and moving. Cut back on time in car seats and bouncers. Helmets still work before 12 months, but earlier is better. After the first birthday, results drop off significantly.

stage4.title: Settling In
stage4.highlights: The top soft spot closes. Head shape is now mostly set. Most minor asymmetries become less obvious as hair grows in.
stage4.tips: Keep up healthy activity habits. If you're still concerned about asymmetry, ask your doctor whether any further steps make sense.

care.title: Daily Care Guide
care.subtitle: Simple, practical ways to support healthy head development

tummyTime.title: Tummy Time
tummyTime.subtitle: Builds strength, prevents flat spots
tummyTime.tip1: Start right after coming home: 3-5 minutes at a time, 2-3 times a day
tummyTime.tip2: Work up to 15-30 min daily by 7 weeks, then 30-40 min by 3 months
tummyTime.tip3: Use toys or a mirror to encourage lifting and looking around
tummyTime.proTip: Chat and sing to your baby during tummy time—it makes the whole thing more fun!

sleep.title: Sleep Position
sleep.subtitle: Safe sleep, balanced shape
sleep.tip1: Always on their back—it's the safest way to sleep (prevents SIDS)
sleep.tip2: Switch which way baby's head faces each night
sleep.tip3: Rotate the crib in the room from time to time
sleep.tip4: Don't let baby spend too long in car seats or bouncers
sleep.warning: Skip the shaping pillows! Pediatric groups warn against any pillows for infants—they're a suffocation risk.

feeding.title: Mix Up Feeding Positions
feeding.subtitle: Balance pressure, support development
feeding.intro: Where baby's head rests during feeding matters. Switching positions helps prevent flat spots.
feeding.tip1: Try different holds: cradle, football, side-lying
feeding.tip3: If there's already a flat spot, keep that side facing up during feeds
feeding.tip4: Notice if baby always turns one way—this could signal torticollis
feeding.tip5: Variety reduces one-sided pressure and helps both eyes develop evenly

environment.title: Set Up the Room
environment.subtitle: Let curiosity do the work
environment.intro: Babies naturally turn toward interesting things. Use this to encourage looking both ways.
environment.tip1: Put toys and mobiles on the rounder side to draw baby's gaze that direction
environment.tip2: Position the crib so baby faces the room when turning toward the rounder side
environment.tip3: Every few days, switch which end of the crib baby's head is at
environment.tip4: Cut back on time in car seats, bouncers, and carriers—they press on the back of the head
environment.tip5: Hold baby often: upright on your shoulder or tummy-down on your arm gives their head a rest

mattress.title: Choosing a Mattress
mattress.subtitle: Firm and safe
mattress.intro: The right mattress matters for both safety and head shape.
mattress.tip1: It needs to be firm and flat—no dent when baby lies down
mattress.tip2: No memory foam, pillow-tops, or soft pads—these raise suffocation risk
mattress.tip3: Make sure it fits snugly in the crib with no gaps (two fingers max at the edge)
mattress.tip4: Use only a fitted sheet—nothing else in the crib
mattress.tip5: Check it regularly and replace if it's sagging or worn

brainDevelopment.title: Does Flat Head Affect Brain Development?
brainDevelopment.subtitle: What the research actually says
brainDevelopment.intro: This is probably the #1 question parents ask. The good news: in most cases, there's nothing to worry about.
brainDevelopment.point1: Mild to moderate positional flat head (plagiocephaly, brachycephaly) does NOT affect brain development or intelligence
brainDevelopment.point2: These are cosmetic changes—they don't reduce brain volume or impair neurological function
brainDevelopment.point3: Studies show no causal link between positional flat head and cognitive problems
brainDevelopment.warning: Important: Pathological conditions like craniosynostosis (premature suture closure) CAN affect brain development and need prompt medical attention. If flat head comes with developmental delays, see a doctor right away.
brainDevelopment.conclusion: Bottom line: mild flat spots are a cosmetic concern, not a brain development issue. But always rule out underlying conditions.

pillowMyth.title: Can Shaping Pillows Fix Flat Head?
pillowMyth.subtitle: The truth about baby pillows
pillowMyth.intro: You'll see lots of "head-shaping" pillows marketed to worried parents. Here's the reality: newborns don't need pillows at all.
pillowMyth.reason1: A newborn's spine is straight—when lying flat, their back and head are naturally aligned. A pillow bends the neck, pushing the chin toward the chest, which can restrict breathing and increase suffocation risk.
pillowMyth.reason2: There's no scientific evidence that shaping pillows improve head shape. They actually restrict natural movement and create safety hazards.
pillowMyth.reason3: The AAP recommends waiting until at least 12 months—18 months is even better.
pillowMyth.warning: Any pillow marketed to "fix" or "prevent" flat head in infants poses a safety risk. Don't use them.

consult.title: When to See a Doctor
consult.subtitle: Combine what you observe with measurement results to decide if you need professional help

normalSigns.title: Keep Monitoring
normalSigns.sign1: Mild unevenness that's improving with care
normalSigns.sign2: Birth molding that rounds out within days
normalSigns.sign3: Baby hitting milestones and moving well

warningSigns.title: Worth a Check-up
warningSigns.sign1: No improvement after 2-3 months of consistent care
warningSigns.sign3: Baby always turns the same way (could be torticollis)
warningSigns.measurement: Measurement reference: CVAI 7-12% (moderate) with no improvement

urgentSigns.title: See Someone Soon
urgentSigns.sign1: Soft spot is bulging or sunken
urgentSigns.sign2: You can feel a raised ridge on the skull (possible craniosynostosis)
urgentSigns.sign3: Head growing too fast or not at all

improvement.title: How Long Until Head Shape Improves?
improvement.subtitle: Setting realistic expectations
improvement.intro: Head shape improvement takes time and consistency. Knowing what to expect helps you stay the course.

mild.title: Mild Asymmetry
mild.desc: With repositioning and tummy time, you'll usually see noticeable improvement

moderate.title: Moderate Asymmetry
moderate.desc: Requires consistent effort and regular monitoring

severe.title: Severe Asymmetry
severe.desc: If conservative measures don't work, your doctor may recommend helmet therapy

improvement.factors: What affects improvement speed: baby's age (younger = faster improvement), severity of the issue, and how consistently you follow through with care routines.
improvement.helmetIntro: Helmet therapy is effective for moderate to severe cases, but it's not needed for everyone.
improvement.helmetPoint1: Best timing: Start at 4-6 months, finish before 12 months
improvement.helmetPoint2: When it's recommended: Conservative care hasn't helped after 2-3 months, or doctor assessment indicates it's needed
improvement.helmetPoint3: What it involves: Usually 2-4 months of wear, about 23 hours per day
improvement.helmetNote: Helmet therapy requires professional evaluation—don't buy one on your own.

skull.title: How Baby's Skull Works
skull.subtitle: Why head shape can change—and when you have the best chance to help
skull.funFact: At birth, a baby's brain is just 25% of adult size—by age 2, it's 75%! That's why the skull stays soft and flexible.

structure.title: Built to Flex
structure.desc: A baby's skull isn't one solid bone—it's several plates connected by flexible tissue called sutures. This lets the skull expand as the brain grows rapidly.

fontanelles.title: The Soft Spots
fontanelles.desc: The soft spots (fontanelles) are where the skull plates meet. The one at the back closes around 2 months; the larger one on top closes between 12-18 months. Doctors use them to check on baby's health.

growth.title: Rapid Brain Growth
growth.desc: Baby's brain grows fastest in the first year, pushing the skull to expand quickly. The skull needs to stay flexible to keep up.

plasticity.title: Shape Can Change
plasticity.desc: Because the skull is still soft, outside pressure (like sleeping position) can affect its shape. The flip side: you can also use positioning to improve it.

recovery.title: After Birth
recovery.desc: Baby's head often looks a bit squished right after delivery—that's from passing through the birth canal. It usually rounds out in 3-5 days.

headTypes.title: Head Shape Guide
headTypes.subtitle: Learn to recognize different head shapes so you can track your baby's progress

normal.name: Normal Head Shape
normal.desc: Looking from above, a normal head is an even oval—balanced front-to-back and side-to-side. Most babies have heads in the normal range.
normal.char1: Even oval shape when viewed from above
normal.char2: Ears line up on both sides
normal.char3: Forehead and back of head are evenly rounded

plagiocephaly.name: Flat Head (One Side)
plagiocephaly.desc: One side of the back of the head is flatter, giving a parallelogram shape from above. The ear on the flat side often shifts forward. This is the most common positional head shape concern.
plagiocephaly.feature: Flattening on one side, parallelogram shape
plagiocephaly.char1: One side of the back is flatter than the other
plagiocephaly.char2: Ear on the flat side may be pushed forward

brachycephaly.name: Flat Head (Back)
brachycephaly.desc: The entire back of the head is flat, making the head look wide and short. Common when babies spend lots of time on their backs. Tummy time and repositioning help.
brachycephaly.char1: Back of head is uniformly flat
brachycephaly.char2: Head looks wider than it is long

dolichocephaly.name: Long Head Shape
dolichocephaly.desc: The head is longer front-to-back with narrower sides, but skull sutures are normal. Often seen in preemies or babies who sleep on their sides. Repositioning can help.
dolichocephaly.char1: Head is longer than it is wide
dolichocephaly.char2: Skull sutures are open and normal

scaphocephaly.name: Boat-Shaped Head
scaphocephaly.desc: A medical condition where the sagittal suture (top of head) closes too early, creating a long narrow head with a bony ridge. This needs surgical treatment and won't improve with positioning alone.
scaphocephaly.feature: Long narrow shape due to early suture closure
scaphocephaly.char1: Bony ridge running along top of head

craniosynostosis.title: ⚠️ Craniosynostosis
craniosynostosis.desc: A rare condition where one or more skull sutures close too early, causing abnormal head growth. Unlike positional flat head, this needs medical evaluation and may require surgery.
craniosynostosis.sign1: Hard ridge along a suture line
craniosynostosis.sign3: Head growth doesn't follow normal pattern
